hints: Look at the two numbers already filled in for expected individuals - 225 and 75. What simple whole-number relationship links 225 to 75?

Remember that an F1 dihybrid EeNn x EeNn cross gives four phenotype classes in a fixed Mendelian proportion when genes are unlinked. Use that proportion to fill the two missing numbers and the two missing ratios.
walkthrough:
Work Out What F1 Flies Look Like**
Both parents are homozygous for both genes, so red normal must be EENN and purple vestigial must be eenn. All F1 offspring receive EN from one parent and en from the other, so all F1 are EeNn with red eyes and normal wings because E and N are dominant.

Apply the Standard Dihybrid Expectation**
An EeNn x EeNn cross with unlinked autosomal genes gives phenotypes in the ratio $9:3:3:1$ - 9 red normal : 3 red vestigial : 3 purple normal : 1 purple vestigial. Since 225 corresponds to 9 parts and 75 corresponds to 3 parts, the missing values are 75 for red vestigial (3 parts) and 25 for purple vestigial (1 part), with missing ratios 9 and 3.

Final answer: Expected number of individuals: red eye, vestigial wing = 75; purple eye, vestigial wing = 25. Expected F2 ratio: red eye, normal wing = 9; purple eye, normal wing = 3. Full expected series is 9:3:3:1.

hints: Start by working out the genotype of the F1 flies from part (a)(i) and the genotype of a fly that is homozygous recessive for both genes.
Think about what different gametes each parent in this test cross can make if the genes assort independently.
Pair one gamete from each parent to build the four offspring genotypes - remember one parent can only make one type of gamete.
For the last mark, link each offspring genotype back to its visible traits using E = red, e = purple, N = normal, n = vestigial.
walkthrough:
State the Parental Genotypes**
The F1 fly is heterozygous for both genes, EeNn, showing both dominant traits. It is crossed to the homozygous recessive, eenn, showing both recessive traits. Write: EeNn x eenn.

List the Gametes With Circles**
Because the investigator assumes independent assortment, the EeNn parent makes four gamete types in equal numbers: EN, En, eN and en. The eenn parent can only make en gametes. Circle or underline the gametes to show they are haploid.

Combine to Give Offspring Genotypes**
Join each F1 gamete with en: EN + en gives EeNn, En + en gives Eenn, eN + en gives eeNn, en + en gives eenn. This predicts a 1:1:1:1 genotypic ratio.

Link Each Genotype to Its Phenotype**
Any genotype with E- has red eyes and ee has purple eyes. Any genotype with N- has normal wings and nn has vestigial wings. So EeNn = red normal, Eenn = red vestigial, eeNn = purple normal, eenn = purple vestigial.

Final answer: Parents: EeNn (F1 red, normal) x eenn (purple, vestigial). Gametes: EN, En, eN, en from EeNn x en from eenn. Offspring genotypes: EeNn, Eenn, eeNn, eenn in equal 1:1:1:1 expectation. Offspring phenotypes: EeNn = red eye, normal wing; Eenn = red eye, vestigial wing; eeNn = purple eye, normal wing; eenn = purple eye, vestigial wing.

hints: Recombinants carry new combinations like E with n, or e with N. These new chromosome combinations are created during meiosis in the F1 parent, not by fertilisation.
Focus on the stage when homologous chromosomes pair closely together and can swap matching sections of chromatids.
walkthrough:
Name the Correct Meiotic Stage**
New allele combinations are created when homologous chromosomes are paired as bivalents. This pairing and exchange happens in prophase I of meiosis in the cells that will form gametes in the F1 fly.

Explain How Exchange Creates Recombinants**
In prophase I, non-sister chromatids of a homologous pair break and rejoin, swapping segments containing E/e and N/n. This crossing over at chiasmata puts E with n and e with N on the same chromatid, so some gametes, and therefore offspring, show the recombinant phenotypes red vestigial and purple normal.
Final answer: Prophase I of meiosis; by crossing over (formation of chiasmata) between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes, producing recombinant chromatids / gametes.

hints: Compare the numbers in Table 2.2 - 196 and 175 are very large, while 22 and 23 are very small. Which phenotypes match the original parents?
If genes were on different chromosomes they would assort independently to give 1:1:1:1. Think about what physical arrangement would keep parental combinations together most of the time.
walkthrough:
Read the Pattern in Table 2.2**
Parental types red normal (196) and purple vestigial (175) are far more common than recombinants red vestigial (22) and purple normal (23). This is not the 1:1:1:1 expected for unlinked genes.

Link the Pattern to Chromosome Behaviour**
The E and N alleles entered the F1 together from one parent and e and n together from the other. Because the two loci are on the same chromosome, these allele sets stay together during meiosis unless crossing over separates them. Without independent assortment, most gametes are parental EN and en, giving the large excess of parental phenotypes.

Final answer: The two genes are linked on the same chromosome (autosomal linkage), so parental alleles E with N and e with n tend to be inherited together; independent assortment does not occur, so parental phenotypes are frequent and recombinants from crossing over are rare.
